Reservoir computing (RC) is a computational framework that utilizes a nonlinear, memory-based kernel to
map time series inputs into a high-dimensional space for information processing. Most hardware-based RC
systems treat their physical reservoirs as black boxes, with the roles of their complex nonlinear dynamics
empirically understood and adjusted by tuning physical conditions. However, theoretically understanding the
reservoir’s nonlinearity in relation to its computational capabilities is crucial for ensuring consistent performance
and adaptive system design. In this paper, we propose a magnetization-saturation-based physical reservoir with
interpretable nonlinearity, where spin dynamics follows a hyperbolic tangent function and its nonlinear scaling
is analytically governed by the damping constant of the magnetic material. Our spin reservoir consists of a
magnetic thin ﬁlm segmented into multiple subregions with different damping constants. This design enables not
only nonlinearity diversity through a variety of nonlinear scaling but also short-term memory through hysteresis
interactions of neighboring spins. We numerically validate our spin RC by demonstrating its high performance in
nonlinear waveform transformation and temporal exclusive-OR (XOR) tasks, which aligns with our theoretical
understanding of the system. We expect this work to contribute to the advancement of reliable and conﬁgurable
spintronic RC systems.

I. INTRODUCTION
Reservoir computing (RC) is a machine learning frame-
work consisting of an input layer, a reservoir layer, and
a readout layer [1,2]. The reservoir layer functions as a
memory-based nonlinear kernel that maps time series inputs
into a high-dimensional space to disclose underlying features.
A readout layer linearly combines the high-dimensionally
mapped information to generate system outputs. Because the
reservoir layer is free from training but only the linear readout
layer is trained, this framework signiﬁcantly reduces the train-
ing complexity compared to other neural network systems. A
well-known example of software-based RC is the echo state
network, which uses a ﬁxed, randomly connected recurrent
neural network as the reservoir layer [3].
Because of the untrained nature of the reservoir, hardware-
based RC has recently been proposed, utilizing physical
systems or phenomena as physical reservoirs to realize higher
processing speed, lower power consumption, and improved
scalability [2]. Physical RC has been explored numerically
and experimentally in various ﬁelds, including electron-
ics [4–6], optics [7,8], and spintronics [9–11]. Among these
candidates, spintronic reservoirs stand out due to their rich dy-
namics, environmental resilience, energy efﬁciency, and fast

Spin is an intrinsic quantum mechanical property of
electrons, associated with their angular momentum. In
magnetic materials, the collective dynamics of spin align-
ments are governed by the Landau-Lifshitz (LL) equa-
tion [14,15]. Various spintronic RC systems have been
studied, exploiting diverse phenomena of spins, such as spin-
torque oscillators [10,16,17], nonlinear spin waves [9,18–20],
skyrmions [11,21–23], and others [24,25].
However, the nonlinear dynamics and properties of these
systems are typically interpreted through empirical investiga-
tions based on their task performance. For example, Ref. [26]
successfully elucidated the inﬂuence of a spin-wave-based
reservoir’s nonlinear behaviors due to boundary reﬂections
on its computational capabilities, yet the underlying spin
dynamics remained difﬁcult to fully comprehend. Similarly,
Ref. [23] demonstrated a successful task-adaptive reservoir
by empirically tuning temperatures and external magnetic
ﬁelds to identify optimal magnetic phases for different tasks,
though the speciﬁc relationship between these parameters and
reservoir behavior remains less understood. These points may
hinder the reservoir design, conﬁguration, and optimization
for speciﬁc tasks, as the reservoir behavior is less controllable
and predictable. Thus, theoretical interpretations of the reser-
voir’s nonlinear dynamics can be crucial for ensuring reliable
computational capabilities and enabling quantitative system
conﬁguration.
In this paper, we propose an on-chip spin reservoir with
interpretable nonlinearity. We utilize the temporal spin dy-
namics of magnetization saturation, which is characterized
by an input-output relationship of a hyperbolic tangent

Figures 2(b) and 2(e) respectively illustrate their spin tra-

they would in the absence of interactions. This observation
is qualitatively elucidated as follows, where the spin m(2) in

from state A to state D in a complete cycle. In state A, m(2)
starts its up-to-down precession in response to a downward
applied ﬁeld ha,z(t). Because m(2) has a damping constant
α2 > α1 and thus a larger scaling factor of saturation in (10)
and (11), m(2) initially has a more positive mz value than
neighboring spins m(1) in Region 1. Therefore, m(2) experi-
ences a propelling interaction from neighboring spins m(1),
facilitating its downward precession. This leads to the spin
trajectory of m(2) in state A lying below the trajectory it would
follow without interaction. As the up-to-down precession con-
tinues to state B, m(2) reaches a more negative mz than m(1),
due to the faster saturation rate associated with its larger α.
As a result, exchange interactions from m(1) begin to resist
the downward precession of m(2). This causes asymmetry
in the slopes of the up-to-down precession trajectory, contrary
to the odd-symmetric slopes observed in no-interaction tra-
jectories. In state C, m(2) initiates its down-to-up precession
in response to an upward ha,z(t). Similar interactions occur,
where the upward precession of m(2) is initially facilitated
by m(1) in state C and is then resisted in state D. Thus, the
down-to-up precession trajectory lies above the no-interaction
trajectory, leading to hysteresis behavior in the spin dynamics.

Consequently, as will be demonstrated in Sec. IV, this not
only enriches nonlinearity in spin dynamics with even-order
nonlinearities but also introduces short-term memory property
for effective temporal information processing in the reservoir.

IV. RESERVOIR PROPERTIES
This section serves as a bridge between our theoretical
analyses of spin dynamics of magnetization saturation and
the effectiveness of our proposed spin reservoir. We conduct
numerical studies to examine the nonlinearity and short-term
memory properties of our spin reservoir, two essential proper-
ties required for RC. To demonstrate the properties provided
by the multi-subregion design, we compare our spin reservoir
to a single-region magnetic ﬁlm of uniform α under the same
physical settings. For conciseness, we use the subregion di-
mension M to distinguish between the two and we focus on
analyses using the example α distribution shown in Fig. 3
for M = 7 and a single region of α = 0.1 for M = 1. Similar
observations are obtained for other α distributions generated
with different random seeds for both M = 7 and M = 1.
We have also conﬁrmed that the hyperbolic tangent re-
lationship described in (10) and (11) under ideal conditions
can be approximately extended to a single-region rectangular-
shaped magnetic thin ﬁlm. Further details are provided in
Appendix B.

V. TASKS AND RESULTS
This section conducts numerical experiments to evaluate
the spin RC’s performance in nonlinear waveform transfor-
mation and temporal XOR operation. These tasks allow us to
validate the proposed spin RC in the following ways:
(1) Nonlinear waveform transformation: This memory-
independent task requires the reservoir to generate speciﬁc
nonlinearities for different target waveforms. Assessing the
RC’s ability to perform these transformations can validate our
understanding of its nonlinearity properties.
(2) Temporal XOR operation: This linearly inseparable
task demands both nonlinearity and short-term memory. Ex-
amining the RC’s ability to solve temporal XOR at different
delay steps can validate the role of its short-term memory in
nonlinear computational problems.
Considering the subregion dimension M as an important
parameter that inﬂuences reservoir properties, we investigate
the performance of spin RCs by varying M = 1, 3, 5, and 7.
We note that increasing M enhances both the diversity in α and
the number of output terminals near subregion boundaries,
thus resulting in reservoir outputs that exhibit greater diversity
with stronger inﬂuences of spin interactions. For each value
of M, we evaluate spin RCs with α distributions generated
from ten different random seeds. The average results across
the ten spin RCs are presented, with error bars indicating their
standard deviations.

VI. DISCUSSION
A. Physical realization of the reservoir
Here, we discuss the physical realization of this on-chip
device. We consider the multi-subregion design with different
values of damping constant α practically realizable via various
techniques, including localized doping [36–38], ﬁlm thickness
variation [39,40], and locally applied laser pulse [41,42]. For
example, Ref. [36] experimentally demonstrated a successful
control of damping in the ferromagnetic alloy (Ga,Mn)As
by doping with different concentrations of Mn ion. Refer-
ence [40] experimentally showed how the damping constant
of a nickel ﬁlm changes as a function of ﬁlm thickness. Refer-
ence [41] provided a dynamic approach to temporarily change
the damping constant of a ferromagnetic thin ﬁlm by using
pump lasers.
The input mechanism is expected to be straightforward to
implement, requiring only a spatially uniform, time-varying
magnetic ﬁeld. The output terminals pose no additional
complexities compared to other spintronic RC systems
that extract spatiotemporal spin information from magnetic
thin ﬁlms [26,43], which can be realized by electrodes
or ﬁlm-penetrating transducers [44]. Additionally, since the

C. Device conﬁgurability
We discuss the conﬁgurability of our device, which in-
cludes the distribution of α values for subregions and the
arrangement of output terminals. In this work, we adopted
a uniform distribution for the conﬁguration of damping con-
stants α. However, depending on the nature of speciﬁc tasks,
optimal α conﬁguration may exist for adaptive design strate-
gies. For example, based on our theoretical understanding of
the spin dynamics in Sec. II, we can conﬁgure the α dis-
tribution with a speciﬁc mean and variance to control the
nonlinearity diversity and the strength of local spin interac-
tions. Furthermore, we can optimally conﬁgure the output
terminals by placing them near or away from subregion
boundaries to alter the inﬂuence of spin interactions, thereby
modifying the system’s nonlinear dynamics and memory
properties. Since these conﬁguration ﬂexibilities are ﬁrmly
rooted in a theoretical understanding of the system, we expect
the spin RC to be reliably adaptable to meet different task
requirements.
VII. CONCLUSION
In conclusion, we proposed a spin reservoir with inter-
pretable nonlinearity. This reservoir is based on odd-order
nonlinear spin dynamics of magnetization saturation, ana-
lytically described by a hyperbolic tangent function with
its scaling governed by the damping constant. Local spin
interactions introduce asymmetric spin dynamics with hys-
teresis behavior to magnetization saturation, which translates
into the enriched even-order nonlinearities and the enhanced
short-term memory properties of the spin reservoir. Lever-
aging this interpretability, we employed a multi-subregion
design of the spin reservoir to effectively enhance both its
nonlinearity diversity and short-term memory, two essen-
tial properties for a robust RC system. We evaluated our
spin RC through numerical experiments, including nonlin-
ear waveform transformation and temporal XOR tasks, with
results validating our theoretical understanding of the sys-
tem. The spin RC exhibits high performance in both tasks,
